###### **About the Editors**

**Dr.** **Bishwajeet** **Pandey** is a professor at GL Bajaj Institute of Technology
and Management, Greater Noida, India. He has been a senior member of
IEEE since 2019. He holds an MTech in Computer Science from the IIIT,
Gwalior, India, and a PhD in Computer Science from the Gran Sasso Science Institute, Italy. He has taught at esteemed institutions such as Chitkara
University, Chandigarh; Jain University, Bangalore; Astana IT University,
Kazakhstan; Eurasian National University, Kazakhstan (QS World Rank 321);
Walsh College, USA; and UCSI University, Malaysia (QS World Rank 265).
He is a prolific researcher with over 30 published books and more than 220
research papers indexed in Scopus. He has garnered over 4400+ citations. His
leadership roles include serving as the research head of the School of CSE at
Jain University, Bangalore, from 2021 to 2023 and as the head of the International Global Academic Partnership Committee at Birla Institute of Applied
Science, Bhimtal, from 2020 to 2021. In 2023, Dr. Pandey was honored with
the prestigious Professor of the Year Award at Lord’s Cricket Ground by the
London Organisation of Skills Development. Beyond his outstanding research
output, his greatest strength lies in his global academic network. He has visited
49 countries, participated in 105 international conferences, and co-authored
papers with 218 professors from 93 universities across 42 nations.

**Advait Patel** is a senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, where he leads the
design and implementation of secure, scalable cloud infrastructure across global
SaaS platforms. With experience in cloud security, DevSecOps, and AI-driven
monitoring systems, he specializes in Kubernetes, Terraform, GCP, and container
security. He is an active member of IEEE and ISACA, a conference speaker, and
the creator of DockSec—an AI-powered Docker security analyzer. He also serves
as a technical reviewer for IEEE and ACM publications and is the author of
multiple cloud security research papers and technical articles.

###### **Preface**

Cloud computing has transformed the way organizations build, deploy, and secure
applications. As enterprises increasingly rely on platforms like Google Cloud,
understanding how to design secure, compliant, and resilient cloud environments
is critical. This book was born out of real-world experience—from securing
large-scale cloud workloads to automating compliance and implementing Zero
Trust architectures.

This book is written for engineers, architects, and security professionals who
want actionable guidance, not just theory. Each chapter blends hands-on practices,
design principles, and real-world examples to help readers confidently secure their
Google Cloud environments.

We hope this book not only serves as a guide but also inspires you to push the
boundaries of what’s possible in cloud security.

_Bishwajeet Pandey_
GL Bajaj Institute of Technology and Management
Uttar Pradesh

_Advait Patel_
Broadcom Inc., United States

###### **1** **Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age** **of AI and Sustainability**

_Karan Alang_ <sup>_1_</sup> _and Anant Kumar_ <sup>_2_</sup>

_1Independent Researcher, Cupertino, CA, USA_
_2Einstein AI Division. Member of IEEE and Sigma Xi, The Scientific Research Honor Society, San Jose,_
_CA, USA_

**1.1** **Introduction**

Cloud computing has undergone a radical transformation since its inception.
It started as a flexible infrastructure for storage and computation but has subsequently transformed to being central to digital transformation initiatives across
nearly every industry.

The convergence of two dominant forces—artificial intelligence (AI) and
sustainability—requires a reassessment of how cloud infrastructure is built, operated, and governed. It requires a reassessment of how cloud computing can play
an even more important role in providing the benefits of AI to various industries.

This chapter introduces understanding this transformation and sets the stage
for the themes that will be explored throughout this book.

Before we dive into AI and sustainability, we will first examine the historical
evolution of cloud computing.

**1.2** **The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From**
**Mainframes to AI-Powered Everything**

**1.2.1** **From Mainframes to Virtualization**

Contrary to popular belief, cloud computing didn’t start with Amazon or
Google. Its roots go way back to 1960, when DARPA threw $2 million at MIT’s
Project MAC—which sounds like loose change today but was serious money

**2** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

back then. The goal is “developing a computer to be used by two or more people,
simultaneously” [1].

Think about it—we’re talking about massive mainframes with magnetic tape
memory that took up entire rooms. The idea of sharing these computational beasts
was basically the Stone Age version of what we now call virtualization.

But here’s where it gets interesting. J.C.R. Licklider came along in 1969 with
his wild vision for ARPANET. He called it an “Intergalactic Computer Network”!
He envisioned the future of the internet before anyone really knew where it was
headed. His idea was simple yet profound: everyone interconnected through
computers, accessing information from anywhere [2].

The 1970s saw virtualization really hit its stride; by the 1990s, virtual machines
were becoming the norm rather than the exception. Then in 1997, Professor
Ramnath Chellapa dropped what I consider one of the most prescient definitions
of cloud computing ever: “a new computing paradigm, where the boundaries of
computing will be determined by economic rationale, rather than technical limits
alone” [3].

Economic rationale over technical limits. That’s basically the cloud in a nutshell!

**1.2.2** **When Theory Met Commerce**

The late 1990s and early 2000s—now that’s when things got really interesting.
Salesforce kicked things off in 1999 with their SaaS offering [4]. But the real
game-changer was Amazon Web Services (AWS) launching EC2 in 2006 [5]. Amazon basically said, “Hey, why don’t we rent out some of our massive computing
power?” and this started the democratization of enterprise computing.

Of course, once Amazon proved the model worked, everyone wanted in.
Microsoft rolled out Azure in 2010, bringing their signature hybrid approach and
deep enterprise integration [6]. Google came to the party with Google Cloud Platform (GCP), throwing their weight behind containerization and Kubernetes [7].

Then you had IBM and Oracle doing their thing with industry-specific solutions

[8, 9], plus Alibaba Cloud basically conquering Asia [10]. Each player brought
something unique to the table, and suddenly we weren’t just talking about
renting servers anymore. We were talking about AI, multicloud orchestration,
sustainability … the works.

Before cloud computing became popular, organizations had to plan the purchase of physical servers based on projected peak usage. This involved effort to
set them up in data centers as well, and then hoping the projections were accurate so the servers could handle the peak traffic. Over-provisioning was the name
of the game because nobody wanted their website to crash during high-traffic
events like Black Friday. This led to underutilization of resources during nonpeak
periods.

_1.2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Mainframes to AI-Powered Everything_ **3**

**1.2.3** **Modern Cloud Architecture and Service Models**

By 2011, National Institute of Science and Technology (NIST) had gotten their act
together and defined the five essential characteristics of cloud computing [11]. You
know the drill: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling,
rapid elasticity, and measured service. Sounds bureaucratic, but these definitions
actually mattered—they gave everyone a common language.

The ISO folks expanded on this later, describing cloud computing as “a
paradigm for enabling network access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable
physical or virtual resources with self-service provisioning and administration
on-demand” [12].

As shown in Figure 1.1, Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS), Platform-as-a-Service
(PaaS), and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) are the holy trinity of cloud services. Each
one abstracts away different layers of complexity. This abstraction is what made
cloud computing accessible to everyone, not just the big players with dedicated IT
teams.

The growth has been tremendous, driven by data-intensive apps, cheaper internet, and everyone’s desperate need for digital transformation [13]. Small businesses suddenly had access to enterprise-grade infrastructure; startups could scale
without massive upfront investments. Game-changing stuff.

Of course, it hasn’t all been smooth sailing. Security concerns, vendor lock-in,
and compliance headaches—these issues keep Chief Information Officers (CIOs)
up at night [5]. And now with AI workloads demanding ever more performance,
cloud providers are constantly under pressure to innovate while keeping costs
reasonable.

**Figure 1.1** Cloud service models [1].

**4** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

**1.2.4** **The Shifting Cloud Paradigm**

The original cloud promise was pretty straightforward: scalability, cost-efficiency,
and flexibility [14]. But modern enterprises wanted it all—performance,
cost-effectiveness, intelligence, automation, and accountability [15]. And it
needs to be sustainable too, because everyone’s suddenly worried about carbon
footprints [16, 17].

This is where AI comes in, both as cloud computing’s biggest beneficiary and its
primary driver. Think about it: AI needs massive computational power for training those complex models, and the cloud provides exactly that. Meanwhile, AI
is making cloud services smarter—predictive analytics, autonomous operations,
you name it.

It’s a symbiotic relationship that’s spawned some impressive innovations.

**1.2.5** **AI: Cloud’s New Growth Engine**

AI has become both a driver and a beneficiary of cloud computing. The cloud offers
the computational horsepower and scalability needed for training and deploying
complex models, while AI infuses intelligence into cloud services, enabling predictive analytics, autonomous operations, and smarter decision-making.

As shown in Figure 1.2, the symbiotic relationship between AI and cloud has
catalyzed innovations in:

  - **AutoML and AI as a Service:** Have basically democratized machine learning.
Google Cloud AutoML, AWS SageMaker Autopilot, and Azure AutoML—these

**Figure 1.2** AI enhancement is driving growth in cloud computing.

_1.2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Mainframes to AI-Powered Everything_ **5**

platforms let nonexperts build decent models without writing much code.
Time-to-value has plummeted, which is great for business but maybe not so
great for traditional data scientists’ job security.

- **Edge** **AI** **and** **Federated** **Learning:** Are solving the latency problem. Why
send all your data to the cloud when you can process it locally? Google’s
federated learning approach is particularly clever—train models on decentralized data without ever moving that data. Privacy preserved, performance
maintained.

- **AIOps Platforms:** Are the unsung heroes here. Azure Monitor, Google Cloud
Operations Suite, and third-party tools like Dynatrace and Datadog—they’re
using ML to predict infrastructure failures, detect anomalies, and allocate
resources dynamically. It’s like having a crystal ball for your data center.

- **Large Language Models:** OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s PaLM, Meta’s LLaMA, and
others—have democratized the usage of machine learning/AI and have been
instrumental in powering applications like customer service bots and code generation tools. The fact that you can access these capabilities through simple API
calls That’s the cloud doing what it does best.

**1.2.6** **Challenges of Supporting AI Workloads in the Cloud**

Supporting large-scale AI workloads presents substantial challenges. The energy
requirements alone are staggering. Training frontier models can require tens
of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) and cost millions per run

[18]. These computational requirements can have a significant environmental
impact.

Then there’s the performance pressure. AI assistants, live transcription,
and fraud detection—these use cases demand sub-second response times at a
global scale. AWS Inferentia, Google’s TPUv5, and NVIDIA’s Triton Inference
Server—everyone’s racing to build faster inference accelerators [19].

Complexity of supporting AI workloads remains a significant challenge. Model
versioning, reproducibility, and access control in multi-tenant environments—
these are key aspects that need to be managed effectively and planned for. Tools
like MLflow, SageMaker Model Registry, and Vertex AI Model Monitoring [20–22]
can be leveraged to manage the complexity. However, the field and tools are still
evolving, and the best practices need to be fully established.

Moreover, regulations are changing faster than we can keep up. The EU AI
Act and data localization laws in China and India—cloud providers are constantly adapting their infrastructure to comply with regional requirements [23].
The dynamic environment and regulatory changes require constant vigilance
and the operational/design flexibility that would allow adapting to the changing
regulations.

**6** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

**1.2.7** **AI and Cloud Use Cases**

As shown in Figure 1.3, the AI and cloud use cases are extensive and varied, despite
the challenges.

In **healthcare**, large language models (LLMs) are handling triage support and

patient interactions while staying HIPAA-compliant through edge processing

[24]. Imagine having an AI that can pre-screen patients and annotate medical
images—all without sending sensitive data to the cloud.
**Retail** has gone all-in on generative AI for dynamic content, personalized market
ing, and demand forecasting [25]. These systems adapt promotions in real time
based on inventory levels and customer behavior. The conversion rate improvements are pretty remarkable.
**Industrial** **IoT** is where predictive maintenance really shines [26]. Sensors

on manufacturing equipment feed data to edge AI models that can predict
failures before they happen. Just-in-time maintenance isn’t just a buzzword
anymore—it’s saving companies millions in downtime costs.
**Autonomous** **Systems** are the crown jewel of edge AI [27]. Real-time object

detection, navigation, and decision-making—all happening locally while syncing with cloud services for updates and coordination. The safety implications
are huge.
**Finance** might be traditionally conservative, but they’ve embraced AI for fraud

detection and credit scoring [28]. Multicloud pipelines process millions of
transactions in real-time, using both supervised and unsupervised learning.
The accuracy improvements are impressive, even if banks are still cautious
about adopting cutting-edge techniques.

**Figure 1.3** AI and cloud use cases.

_1.3_ _The Sustainability Imperative_ **7**

**Cybersecurity** platforms are using cloud-based Security Information and Event

Management (SIEMs) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) systems
with AI-enhanced threat detection [29, 30]. These systems ingest logs from
everywhere—endpoints, APIs, and network traffic—and flag anomalies faster
than any human analyst could.

As cloud platforms race to deliver AI infrastructure and services, they’re juggling
three critical requirements: performance, cost-efficiency, and compliance. It’s not
easy maintaining agility while embedding sustainability and ethics into everything
you do [31, 32].

**1.3** **The Sustainability Imperative**

Let’s talk about something that’s been keeping a lot of us in the industry up at night
lately. Data centers—those massive, humming temples to our digital age—can be
a bit problematic from an environmental standpoint. It is true that cloud infrastructure still offers unparalleled scalability and flexibility. But it is also a fact that
it consumes a staggering amount of energy.

And then AI came along and basically threw gasoline on the fire.
Training large LLM models like GPT-4, LLaMa 3, Claude 4, and PaLM does take
a lot of resources. We’re talking about “compute” requirements that would make a
supercomputer from the 1990s look very small. These models demand specialized
hardware, extensive data pipelines, and round-the-clock inferencing for real-time
applications. The energy consumption across the entire AI lifecycle is extensive.

The use cases of ML/AI (specifically LLMs) are varied—real-time content generation, AI chatbots, smart search, and autonomous decision systems, to name a few.
Finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity—all domains need and benefit from the AI
advancement, which means cloud workloads are higher than they’ve ever been.

So here we are caught between the promise of AI-powered everything and the
reality that our planet has limits.

In response, the sustainability imperative pushes the cloud industry toward
operational practices and architectural innovations that minimize ecological
impact while maintaining service performance and economic viability.

As highlighted in Figure 1.4, the key AI, cloud, and sustainability strategies
shaping this evolution are discussed below.

1) **Renewable Energy Commitments**
The big players—Google, Microsoft, and Amazon—have made some pretty
bold commitments. Operating entirely on renewable energy by 2030 or earlier.
Solar, wind, hydroelectric, you name it. Microsoft’s pledge to go carbon negative by 2030 and remove all their historical emissions by 2050? That’s not just

**8** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

**Figure 1.4** AI, cloud, and sustainability.

PR speak; they’re actually tracking this stuff with sustainability dashboards
and third-party audits.

Power purchase agreements (PPAs) are becoming the norm rather than the
exception. It’s fascinating to watch these tech giants essentially become major
players in the green energy development game.
2) **Carbon-Aware Workload Scheduling**
Here’s something that’s cleverer than it sounds: carbon-aware workload
scheduling. The idea is beautifully simple—dynamically shift compute jobs
across geographic locations based on real-time carbon intensity data.

Got a machine learning training job that isn’t super urgent? Route it to
the data center where renewable energy is abundant right now. Google
Cloud’s carbon-aware computing platform and Microsoft’s emissions impact
dashboard are making this kind of optimization accessible to customers. It’s
like traffic routing, but for carbon footprints.
3) **Serverless and Ephemeral Computing**
Serverless computing—AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud
Functions—turns out to be an environmental win, not just a developer convenience. When you think about it, it makes perfect sense. These ephemeral
compute environments eliminate idle resource consumption. No more servers
sitting around burning electricity waiting for something to happen.

Event-driven architectures allow for micro-optimizations at runtime, which
is great for both sustainability and your AWS bill. Win-win.
4) **Circular Hardware Lifecycles**
This one’s particularly interesting. Instead of the traditional “buy new,
throw away old” approach, cloud providers are embracing circular economy

_1.4_ _Challenges and Opportunities_ **9**

principles. Refurbishing servers, recycling rare earth metals, and designing
equipment for modularity and extended life.

Google’s 2022 Sustainability Report showed that over 25% of their deployed
servers were refurbished machines. That’s thousands of metric tons of avoided
carbon emissions. Not bad for what basically amounts to smart recycling.
5) **Sustainability by Design**
Rather than bolting sustainability onto existing infrastructure (which, let’s
face it, never works well), modern cloud infrastructure is being designed with
eco-efficiency as a first-class objective. We’re seeing innovations in liquid
cooling to reduce HVAC loads, AI-driven power and thermal management
systems, and data centers co-located with renewable energy sources.

Custom chips like Google’s TPU and AWS’s Graviton processors are optimized for performance per watt. It’s amazing what happens when you design
for efficiency from the ground up rather than trying to retrofit it later.
6) **Transparent Reporting and Green Metrics**
Cloud customers are getting increasingly demanding about visibility into their
environmental impact—and honestly, it’s about time. Providers are publishing
sustainability reports, real-time dashboards, and APIs that offer transparency
on carbon intensity, water usage effectiveness (WUE), and power usage effectiveness (PUE).

Tools like the AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool and the Azure Sustainability Calculator let enterprises actually track and reduce their environmental
impact rather than just hoping for the best. The thing is, this isn’t just about
doing the right thing anymore (though that matters). It’s becoming a competitive differentiator, a driver of innovation, and surprisingly often, a source of
long-term cost savings.

Sustainability, when treated as a design principle rather than a constraint,
can yield not only environmental benefits but also operational efficiency and
cost savings.

**1.4** **Challenges and Opportunities**

Integrating AI and sustainability into cloud ecosystems introduces a complex
landscape of challenges and opportunities that must be navigated thoughtfully to
ensure future-proof architectures.

1) **Managing the Energy-Intensive Nature of Large-Scale AI**
Training large foundation models like GPT and PaLM requires computational
resources that translate directly to high energy consumption and carbon
emissions [33, 34]. We’re talking about training runs that consume as much
electricity as dozens of US households use in a year. For a single model.

**10** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

The response has been interesting, though. Hyperscalers and AI firms
are turning to renewable energy sources, hardware optimization (ASICs like
Google TPUs), and energy-aware scheduling algorithms. It’s not solving the
fundamental problem, but it’s making progress.
2) **Balancing Performance and Eco-Efficiency**
Here’s the rub: achieving high performance for AI workloads often means provisioning extensive computational infrastructure, which directly conflicts with
sustainability goals. Finding the sweet spot between latency, throughput, and
energy usage demands some pretty novel optimization strategies.

Serverless AI architectures are helping. Edge deployment for inference workloads reduces long-distance data transfer and energy consumption. But we’re
still figuring out the optimal approaches.
3) **Ensuring Ethical AI Development and Deployment**
AI models hosted on cloud platforms can exhibit bias, opacity, and unfairness
unless they’re governed by strict ethical standards. Integrating responsible AI practices—explainability, fairness-aware learning, or transparent
documentation—into cloud-based development pipelines is becoming
essential.

And there’s the environmental justice angle too. The impact of siting data
centers in resource-strained communities is something we need to talk about
more openly.
4) **Standardizing Green Cloud Metrics and Benchmarks**
A lack of universal standards for assessing the environmental impact of
cloud-based AI limits progress. There’s a growing call for standardized
sustainability metrics, such as PUE, carbon usage effectiveness (CUE), and
ML-specific emissions per training run. Benchmarking frameworks like
MLPerf must evolve to include eco-efficiency metrics alongside performance
measures.
5) **Opportunities at the Intersection of Technology, Policy, and Ethics**
While the challenges are significant, they also create space for groundbreaking
innovation.
Opportunities include:

    - Green AI research that optimizes models not just for accuracy but also for
carbon footprint

    - AI-powered sustainability applications, such as optimizing power grids,
reducing waste, and improving climate models

    - Policy innovations, such as carbon credits for eco-friendly compute jobs

    - Cross-sector collaborations to set global standards for sustainable AI
deployment

These intersecting trends highlight the importance of a multidisciplinary
approach to building the future of cloud computing.

_1.6_ _Future Scope_ **11**

**1.5** **Conclusion**

In this chapter, we explored the changing face of cloud computing, and how AI and
sustainability have refined how cloud computing architectures are being reimagined. We delved into the evolution of cloud computing from the early roots in
mainframe time-sharing to its current role as a backbone of AI and sustainability
efforts.

We also examined the modern cloud architecture and service models, highlighting how they are evolving to support the demands of AI advancements.
We explored how AI has become the growth engine for cloud computing, with
the symbiotic relationship between the two. We delved into the AI and cloud use
cases, which have seen extensive growth.

While AI has fueled the growth of cloud computing, there are multiple challenges to supporting AI workloads in the cloud. The chapter delved into some
of these challenges. Further, the chapter provided an introduction on the sustainability imperatives and requirements on the cloud computing industry with
the increasing datacenter (i.e., energy) demands for ML model training and inference. The chapter highlights the key “AI, Cloud, and Sustainability” strategies that
companies are adopting to balance performance, cost, and sustainability considerations. Finally, we look at the challenges and opportunities in integrating AI and
sustainability with cloud computing.

In summary, the chapter explores the advancements and synergies of cloud computing, AI, and sustainability and highlights the importance of balancing performance, cost, and ethical considerations in building next-generation cloud systems.
As organizations continue to adopt AI at scale, these themes will become even
more central to how cloud architectures evolve and sustainability becomes a “key”
requirement of how infrastructure is designed and governed.

**1.6** **Future Scope**

In the chapters ahead, we’re going to dive deep into how cloud computing
is being reshaped by AI and sustainability working together. You’ll see how
platforms are evolving to meet demands for intelligent, efficient, and ethical
digital infrastructure.

We’ll explore the transition from basic virtual machines to highly abstracted,
serverless, event-driven architectures. Cloud-native design patterns, microservices, and multicloud strategies—all the stuff that’s making modern infrastructure
both more resilient and more complex.

AI plays the central role throughout this journey, naturally. AI as a service, intelligent automation, AIOps, and the increasingly critical challenge of managing cost
and complexity through FinOps—especially for generative AI workloads that can
burn through budgets faster than you can say “transformer architecture.”

**12** _1_ _Introduction: Reimagining Cloud Computing in the Age of AI and Sustainability_

Security, privacy, and regulatory compliance receive focused attention as well.
Zero Trust architectures, embedded DevSecOps practices, and data localization
laws ensure that as cloud-native threats grow, organizations use proactive security
strategies that strengthen threat detection and cyber resilience.

Then we’ll look toward the future: sustainable architectures that reduce the
environmental impact of AI workloads, the promise and limitations of quantum
computing in the cloud, and using cloud infrastructure for scientific research and
high-performance computing.

Throughout all of this, we’ll maintain a strong ethical lens. Questions of bias,
fairness, and responsible AI deployment—these aren’t nice-to-haves anymore;
they’re fundamental to building systems that work for everyone.

By the end, you’ll have a holistic understanding of how cloud computing is
evolving in the AI age and, more importantly, the practices that will define its
sustainable and secure future.

Because ultimately, reimagining cloud computing through these lenses opens
the door to a future where digital progress actually aligns with ecological and ethical imperatives. And frankly, it’s about time!

###### **2** **The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines** **to Serverless**

_Anuj Ashok Potdar_ <sup>_1_</sup> _and Pronnoy Goswami_ <sup>_2_</sup>

_1IEEE Senior Member, Boston, MA, USA_
_2IEEE Senior Member, Santa Clara, CA, USA_

**2.1** **Introduction**

This section explores how the term “cloud computing” came into existence and
traces its roots from the traditional time-sharing systems and ARPANET in the
1960s [1], followed by the advent of Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) in the 1990s [2],
and finally to the mainstream adoption of the term in the 2000s [3]. It also dives
deep into terms like virtualization, hypervisors, the birth of the modern container
architecture and orchestration, and the serverless paradigms [4, 5].

The chapter also breaks down the NIST definition of cloud computing in detail
and explains each term of the definition with examples [6]. Going through the
historical context and significance, this section covers each development throughout the last 50 years that has laid the foundation of the current cloud computing architecture, highlighting the contributions of various tech companies like
IBM, Salesforce, Google, and Amazon in creating technologies and solutions that
are used in some form or another throughout the world for the deployment and
hosting of their applications [2, 3, 7] and briefly touching on different types of
service models in cloud computing, the SaaS, Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), and
Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS), and the level of flexibility and customization
offered by each of them [8].

Listing various types of virtualizations and the different technologies used
in virtualization and cloud computing, we discuss types of hypervisors, their
advantages, and shortcomings in detail [9]. Finally, we discuss the limitations
of traditional computationally intensive virtualization techniques and how the
modern containerization and serverless architectures provide a much lighter

**16** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

and extensible solution, crucial for modern-day high-speed and high-scale
applications that need to scale up and down on demand as the load increases and
decreases [4, 5, 10].

Going through containerization, we discuss the role of Docker and how it has
led to the ease of development for software engineers to concentrate solely on the
functionality and business needs while developing an application without having to worry about how the application would behave differently in production
compared to the development environment [11].

**2.2** **The Definition of Cloud Computing**

As per the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the definition
of cloud computing is as follows [6]:

_Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand_
_network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources_ … _that_
_can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or_
_service provider interaction_ .

Let us break down the definition to understand it better. Cloud computing
stands for the use of the internet or a network (depending on the type of cloud)
to access computer resources from a shared pool of resources, which can include
resources like servers, databases, and even Graphic Processing Units (GPUs) in
a modern context, without the need to own these resources and their physical
hardware components yourself [6].

The term “ubiquitous” in the definition points to the accessibility aspect of cloud
computing, where a pool of resources can be at any one location and accessed from
a completely different location seamlessly without needing to move it from one
place to another, given that you are connected to the network (often the internet)
that it is hosted on [6].

Additionally, the mention of “rapidly provisioned and released with minimal
management effort” means that the time required to start and stop using these
resources should be less, and there should not be a need for someone to manually
set up these resources for you every time as there is a change in the computational
needs or configuration requirement [6].

This paradigm emphasizes renting. In cloud computing, instead of keeping a
particular piece of hardware permanently, you rent a specific configuration temporarily as needed [4, 6].

_2.3_ _Historical Context and Significance_ **17**

**2.3** **Historical Context and Significance**

Today, we rely heavily on cloud computing, which we often don’t fully understand.
From our Google Photos and Apple iCloud to ChatGPT, everything works on cloud
computing [12]. We use it effortlessly and with a high level of abstraction, which
has made it a crucial part of our lives. It is ubiquitous; we do not spend efforts on
managing whether we need to scale it up or down. Let us go back in time and trace
where the term was originally coined.

The term “cloud computing” first gained widespread popularity in 2006 when
Eric Schmidt, the then CEO of Google, used this term publicly at the Search Engine
Strategies (SES) Conference in San Jose, California, in August 2006 [13]. During
a Q&A session at the conference, he explained Google’s approach to web-based
applications and stated:

_What’s interesting is that there is an emergent new model. I don’t think peo-_
_ple have really understood how big it’s going to be. It starts with the premise_
_that the data services and architecture should be on servers. We call it cloud_
_computing; they should be in a ‘cloud’ somewhere_ [13].

Eric Schmidt’s mention of “cloud computing” at a 2006 tech conference was
one of the first times the term appeared in a high-profile public setting, describing a move away from local software to internet-based services, a concept that
had existed internally for years but only gained mainstream traction after that
moment. However, the modern cloud era truly began later that year when Amazon
Web Services (AWS) launched Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), offering businesses
on-demand access to virtual servers [3]. Although Schmidt popularized the term,
it gained more widespread use in the modern context after the launch of AWS
EC2, where Amazon introduced its infrastructure as a service (IaaS), providing raw
computing power for applications to be built with higher control and flexibility [3].

In 1997, during a lecture at Emory University, Professor Ramnath Chellappa, a
well-known researcher in digital business and technology, introduced the concept
of cloud computing and provided the following definition:

_A computing paradigm where the boundaries of computing will be determined_
_by economic rationale rather than technical limits_ [5].

This definition has been pivotal for a few reasons, mainly because it emphasized
the on-demand access of computing resources and also highlighted the economic
scalability, which is very relevant and important even today.

**18** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

However, the term had been used internally much earlier, but it had not gained
widespread popularity; for example, Compaq had used it internally since 1996.
In a 1996 document entitled “Internet Solutions Division Strategy,” Compaq executives drafted an internal document that referenced “cloud-computing-enabled
applications” [5].

The foundation of this term can be traced back to the 1960s, during the
mainframe era, when the foundation of virtualization was established. In this
period, resources to carry out heavy computation operations were in short supply
because they were very expensive and novel for the time. As necessity is the
mother of invention, this led to the development of systems and strategies used
for time-based sharing systems, facilitating multiple users to access the same
mainframe system simultaneously [7, 14].

**2.4** **Evolution Timeline Overview**

The cloud computing paradigm has evolved over the past few decades, and it has
been evolving ever since. From the early 1960s to the present day, there have been
constant developments in the areas of virtualization, resource sharing, networked
utilities, and distributed systems that have shaped it into what it is today [1, 14].

During the first mentions of cloud computing in 1960s and 1970s in the form of
virtualization, it primarily focused on abstracting physical hardware. In the 1960s’’
Mainframe Era, the computers were huge, and they were primarily owned by
larger entities like government offices, universities, or giant corporations. Because
of these factors, access to computers and their giant computational resources was
limited to a single user, which resulted in a waste of computational power. A solution to this was proposed and designed by projects like MIT’s CTSS (Compatible
Time-Sharing System) in 1961 and followed by Multics in 1965. Both of these
worked on the concept of time-sharing that allowed multiple users to access the
same mainframe computer simultaneously, which in turn reduced the idle time
for the machines and facilitated resource pooling, which is a core cloud computing
principle [14].

The ARPANET, which is the precursor to the modern-day internet, was developed in 1969 as a project of the U.S. Defense Department that connected computers
across different locations. This has been pivotal in demonstrating the power and
potential of networked resources, where the resources can be in various places
and still be provided with “ubiquitous access” [1]. This also led to the foundation
of remote job entry (RJE), which allows users to submit their tasks to the mainframe over a network, similar to how APIs work in today’s cloud services [1].

With the advent of the UNIX operating system during the 1970s, developed
at Bell Labs, along with it came the multi-user, multi-tasking architecture and

_2.4_ _Evolution Timeline Overview_ **19**

the ability to run on various hardware, which influenced future cloud-friendly
operating systems like Linux [10]. Decentralized computing was getting explored
by projects like Xerox PARC’s Alto (1973) and Ethernet (1973) that primarily
worked on decentralized computing, which allows resources to be shared across
networked machines [10]. Concepts like virtual memory came into existence,
allowing and enabling programs to use more memory than what was physically available, all of which has been a precursor to the modern-day distributed
cloud architecture [10].

In the 1990s, the World Wide Web (1991) was launched, and it transformed
the internet from a niche academic tool into a full-fledged commercial platform.
This introduced HTTP for transferring data and HTML for structuring the content
on the web. Alongside came some other inventions that aided the growth of information transfer like Common Gateway Interface scripts (CGI, 1993) for dynamic
web content, JavaScript (1995) for client-side interactivity to browsers, and Java
(1995) for platform-independent applets that could run in browsers [5].

Server-side innovations occurred during this era. Open-source technologies like
Apache became a key contributor to empowering over 50% of the websites by
1996 [5]. Hypertext Preprocessor (PHP) (1994–1995) allowed the software to have
embedded logic directly into HTML, and it simplified the creation and enhanced
the usage of dynamic web applications [5].

The Dot-Com Boom happened, and businesses raced to be a part of it, which created a demand for scalable software solutions. Companies like Salesforce emerged
that primarily focused on changing the way people used to consume software,
changing the mode of software delivery from on-premise software like Microsoft
Office and Oracle databases, which required expensive licenses, installation, and
IT maintenance, into a more portable solution delivered directly through the web
browser. This helped reduce the cost and time to get up and running, and this was
the birth of the modern-day SaaS model, most commonly referred to as SaaS [2].
Small businesses could pay a monthly subscription fee rather than an expensive
license, which made this model even more popular.

Even though SaaS became popular for using software, for building their
software, many companies still relied on physical servers, managed hosting, and
colocation, which required a lot of physical space, hiring people, and building
infrastructure, and scaling up would require a huge amount of investment for
increasing the server space and capacities. This used to be a huge bottleneck,
especially when a smaller web application gained overnight popularity and the
servers were not enough to handle the increased load and requests [3].

This problem was addressed during the Modern Cloud Era (2006–2010), during
which PaaS and IaaS started gaining increasing popularity. The key invention
of virtualization decoupled software from hardware, which in turn allowed
platforms to be turned into a self-service, Application Programming Interface

**20** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

(API)-driven utility [4, 8]. One such key platform is AWS, launched in March
2006. AWS unveiled S3 (Simple Storage Service), which worked on RESTful
APIs to provide standard GET/PUT commands to access storage over HTTP [3].
Companies building software could now store their data on AWS just by interacting with a GET and PUT request. They also introduced EC2 (Elastic Cloud
Compute), which enabled on-demand virtual machine (VM) instances with root
access and was the first true IaaS, allowing developers to rent compute power
by the hour [3]. Microsoft launched Windows Azure in 2008 (later rebranded
as Microsoft Azure in 2014), focusing on PaaS for .NET developers, then later
pivoted to IaaS in 2010 by introducing Windows Server VMs [3]. Similarly, Google
offered its cloud solution through Google Cloud Platform (GCP) with the App
Engine in 2008, offering a sandboxed PaaS where developers could deploy Python
and Java applications. GCP expanded to IaaS with Google Compute Engine (GCE)
in 2012 with an open-source hypervisor for Linux/Windows VMs [3].

In 2013, with the advent of Docker, the containerization revolution began,
which provided a more lightweight and portable alternative to traditional
VMs [11]. These platforms transformed the software architecture paradigms by
enabling microservices, DevOps, and the cloud-native movement [4, 15]. Each
one of these innovations has increased the levels of abstraction and automation,
slowly and gradually freeing software developers from their focus on infrastructure and concentrating more on building the functionality. Finally, serverless
computing emerged in 2014 with AWS Lambda, further abstracting infrastructure
management and enabling a pure focus on code [4, 15].

**2.5** **The Foundations: Virtual Machines and Early**
**Virtualization**

**2.5.1** **The Concept of Virtualization**

Virtualization is the backbone of cloud computing, the process of abstracting and
creating software-based demarcations of physical computing resources [6]. NIST
defines virtualization as follows:

_Virtualization is the simulation of the software and/or hardware upon which_
_other software runs. It allows multiple operating systems and applications to_
_run on the same physical hardware_ [6].

Let us break down the definition to understand it better. Simulation of the software refers to creating a virtual version of an entire operating system or application
environment that mimics the behavior of a real one. Hardware simulation refers
to emulating physical computer components like CPUs, memory, and storage. In a
very oversimplified language, we can think of it as one or more logical computers

_2.5_ _The Foundations: Virtual Machines and Early Virtualization_ **21**

inside a real computer. This hardware or software virtualization system behaves
just like a real machine, and the software running on top of it can run as if it is running on an independent machine. In a non-virtualized or traditional computing
environment, one operating system controls one physical machine, but virtualization breaks this limitation by allowing multiple VMs to run on one physical
machine, and each VM thinks it has its dedicated hardware [8].

The core idea of virtualization revolves around the abstraction of physical
resources, enabling multiple environments on the same hardware. The concept
of virtualization started in the 1960s–1970s with the early mainframe era. IBM
invested heavily in developing IBM CP-40 (1967) and CP/CMS (later renamed as
VM/CMS), which introduced hypervisors that allowed a single mainframe to host
multiple independent VMs [7]. Time sharing and resource pooling allowed CPU
time, memory, and storage to be dynamically allocated to users, creating a facade
of dedicated machines while sharing the dedicated underlying hardware [7].

Virtualization in a cloud context is offered in four prominent verticals [8, 9]:

- Server Virtualization

- Storage Virtualization

- Network Virtualization

- GPU Virtualization

The invention of full virtualization enabled each VM to have the ability to run
its operating system and applications. Most importantly, they were isolated from
each other, which allowed running applications of different natures on the same
hardware. This resulted in significant improvements in resource utilization and
cost-effectiveness, positioning cloud computing as an attractive option for software deployment [4, 8]. Another key advantage of virtualization is how it offers
disaster recovery and portability. In the event of a site failure, VM snapshots and
live migration enable seamless recovery [4, 8].

**2.5.2** **Hypervisor—Virtual Machine Technology Explained**

Let us take a minute to understand a little bit about hypervisors. Hypervisors
are the monitors of VMs. They are software layers that are used for creating and
managing VMs by performing operations like allocation of physical hardware
resources to each VM while keeping the isolation, security, and fairness between
the VMs [9].

There are two main types of hypervisors, and this section will go through both
of them in detail:

- _Type-1 Hypervisor, also known as Bare-Metal Hypervisor:_
This hypervisor runs directly on the physical hardware, without the need for a
host OS. It offers higher performance and security and is used in enterprise data
centers and cloud computing [9].

**22** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

Since there is no underlying operating system layer, they offer near-native
performance, making the overhead minimal while also focusing on
strong isolation and providing direct hardware access, which is crucial for
high-performance workloads [9]. Examples are VMware ESXi, Microsoft
Hyper-V, Xen, and kernel-based VM (KVM) [9].

   - _Type-2 Hypervisor, also known as the Hosted Hypervisor:_
This hypervisor runs on top of a conventional operating system such as
Windows, macOS, or Linux. It is commonly used for development and testing
on various platforms without having to invest in purchasing different hardware [9]. The presence of a host OS makes it easy to install and use this type
of hypervisor, which is a great solution for running multiple OSes on a single
machine [9].

However, due to the presence of a host OS, the performance suffers as there
is a higher overhead, and it is less secure, as a compromise in the host OS
will affect all the VMs hosted on it [9]. Examples are Oracle VirtualBox, VMware
Workstation/Fusion, and Parallels Desktop [9].

**2.5.3** **The Transition from Physical to Virtual Infrastructure**

Before virtualization, in an enterprise setting, each application was bound to
one server. The servers were powerful and expensive machines, often dedicated
to a single critical application. Needless to say, this approach was proven to
be very cost-intensive with a lack of resource utilization; each machine would
run at 15–20% of the server’s CPU, memory, and I/O capacity, causing huge
amounts of expensive computing power to be idle. This represented significant amounts of wasted capital expenditure, and beyond the hardware cost, this
inefficiency resulted in several other problems as well, namely:

   - **Data** **Center** **Footprints:** Underutilized servers demanded enormous space
and would require a higher number of servers to fulfill the enterprise server
demands.

   - **High Power and Cooling Costs:** Each physical server, irrespective of the workload or idle time, would consume significant electricity and generate a high
amount of heat that requires expensive cooling.

   - **Lack of Operational Flexibility:** Adding a new physical server was a slow and
labor-intensive task, involving procurement, physical racking, cabling, installation of the operating system, and configuration, which could take weeks or
months, making resource scaling equally painful.

   - **Difficult** **Disaster** **Recovery:** In case of loss of physical servers, recovery/
restoration would rely on complex, slow, and often unreliable backup/restore
processes.

_2.6_ _The Birth of Modern Cloud Computing_ **23**

Virtualization greatly counters these constraints using hypervisors, where
each VM operates like a self-contained physical computer running its own
operating system and applications. Also, multiple VMs can be hosted on a single
physical host server, which further helps in reducing the amount of physical
hardware required. Some of the key enablers of the virtualization concepts
are hardware-assisted virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V), which uses CPU
extensions to significantly reduce the performance overhead of the hypervisor by
handling complex privilege-level translations, and mature hypervisor software
(ESX/ESXi) developed by companies like VMware, Xen, Microsoft Hyper-V, and
KVM that provide robust, enterprise-level management and features.

All of these techniques provide a lot of cost efficiency by consolidating _n_ number
of physical servers into a single powerful host, which helps reduce the idle time
and dramatically improves the hardware resource utilization. This reduced the
CapEx by having fewer physical servers that needed to be purchased, and reduced
operational expenses were significantly reduced by optimizing power consumption, cooling requirements, and data center real estate space.

Despite the benefits and various features, enterprise adoption was not easy;
there were significant challenges to be addressed. With the early hypervisors
(especially without hardware assist), performance overhead concerns were very
prevalent, as they had measurable overheads. Enterprise software architects
would often be concerned about the impact of virtualization on large databases
and transaction systems and whether consolidating multiple VMs on a single
physical hardware would hurt system performance. Compatibility issues among
applications and hardware peripherals would cause some of these not to interact
well with each other.

**2.6** **The Birth of Modern Cloud Computing**

**2.6.1** **Limitations of Traditional Virtual Machines**

The traditional VMs were great for the time, but as computing started becoming
heavier and demand increased, certain challenges and limitations were observed.
This section will go through each limitation and challenge in detail:

- _Resource Overhead_
Traditional VMs require a full operating system instance, which consumes substantial memory and storage even when idle and not in use. In high-density
environments where resource utilization is maximum, this becomes even more
problematic [4].

Let us take an example to understand this better. Consider a host that is
running 20 VMs on it, with each VM instance consuming 1 GB of RAM, which

**24** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

could waste up to 20 GB of RAM just on OS kernels. In such a configuration,
high-density microservices that have hundreds of instances would become
infeasible [4].

   - _Slow Startup Times_
Traditional VMs also suffered from slow startup and boot times, which would
take up minutes of boot time, something that is unacceptable in today’s computing scenario, where we sometimes need to scale up for handling sudden traffic
spikes due to unexpected increased usage [4].

The complete process of traditional VM boot involves steps like BIOS/UEFI
initialization, hypervisor hardware checks, and full OS kernel initialization. This
makes serverless functions that require less than 100 ms initialization impossible to achieve [4].

   - _Operational Complexity_
With multiple operating systems across all the VMs on the host, their management becomes an administrative burden. Here, a system administrator would
be required to manage each VM OS individually [4].

It was impossible to have 2 applications that require 2 different versions of
a dependency to be deployed on the same VM; this would lead to dependency
conflicts, security overhead, and admin burden [4].

   - _Deployment and Portability Challenges_
The most important and biggest challenge faced by traditional VMs was deployment and portability. Applications that were developed in one environment
would often behave differently when deployed to production systems due to
configuration differences between their environments [4, 8].

Applications would fail if the host hypervisor were not similar to the development environment’s kernel versions. Library dependency, network/firewall
rules, and storage configuration mismatches were among other problems that
would cause “mystery failures” in the production environment [4, 8].

All these limitations and challenges collectively paved the way for the container revolution, which introduced a lighter approach to virtualization [4, 11].

**2.6.2** **The Rise of Containerization**

To overcome the limitations of traditional VMs, containerization came into
existence. The approach of containerization is a revolutionary one, where
application deployment was transformed from the traditional isolation concept
into a cloud-native superpower. In 1979, Unix introduced “chroot,” which
allowed a form of filesystem isolation [10]. During the early 2000s, technologies
like FreeBSD Jails and Solaris Containers added further isolation capabilities,

_2.6_ _The Birth of Modern Cloud Computing_ **25**

which helped in orchestrating this technology [10]. Building on all these technologies, in 2013, with the introduction of Docker, the term “containerization”
achieved mainstream acceptance and adoption [11]. Docker’s approach was very
developer-friendly; it transformed containers from a complex and specialized
technology into an accessible tool for machines. The core differentiator of Docker
containers from VMs is that, unlike a VM, which virtualizes the entire hardware
stack along with the operating systems, containers virtualize at the operating system level, allowing them to share the host’s kernel and use namespaces and control
groups (cgroups) technologies to maintain isolation among containers [11].

This architectural paradigm difference allows a container to be extremely light
compared to VMs, in the order of megabytes rather than gigabytes, and allows a
quick start-up time in the order of seconds, or if of a lower complexity, then even
milliseconds [11]. This has revolutionized application deployment by ensuring
consistency across development, testing, and production environments, also
dramatically improving resource utilization and making applications truly
portable [11].

**2.6.3** **Container Orchestration**

With the increasing adoption of containers, managing large numbers of them has
become a challenge. Since manually managing containers became impractical,
container orchestration platforms rose to address the complex challenges of
deploying, scaling, networking, and maintaining containerized applications at
scale [16].

In 2014, Google introduced Kubernetes, leveraging its experience running
containerized workloads via its Borg system [16]. Through the use of a strong
mechanism for automated deployment and for scaling and load balancing, the
platform’s architecture consists of a control plane that manages the cluster
state in addition to worker nodes that run the containerized applications; this
architecture creates a powerful but complex system for managing containerized
environments [16]. Notably, Docker Swarm gave a simpler alternative, smoothly
integrating with Docker, while Apache Mesos gave wider, general-purpose cluster
management capabilities to run containers besides workloads [16]. Other cloud
providers have developed managed Kubernetes services such as Amazon EKS,
Google Kubernetes Engine, and Azure Kubernetes Services that work for reducing
the complexity of maintaining orchestration platforms [16].

The container orchestration model has fundamentally transformed the applications deployed and managed within cloud environments. It has also enabled
organizations to operate on a scale that was previously impossible [16].

**26** _2_ _The Evolution of Cloud Computing: From Virtual Machines to Serverless_

**2.7** **The Serverless Paradigm**

**2.7.1** **The Concept of Serverless Computing**

Serverless computing represents a transformative advancement in cloud architecture, significantly reshaping traditional approaches to application deployment and
management. Despite its nomenclature, “serverless” does not imply the absence of
servers; instead, it encapsulates the abstraction of server management away from
developers. In this paradigm, developers exclusively focus on crafting application
logic, while cloud service providers manage infrastructure provisioning, scaling,
security, and maintenance responsibilities [17, 18].

The foundational principles of serverless computing include infrastructure
abstraction, ephemeral compute instances triggered only when necessary, an
event-driven execution model, and a consumption-based pricing structure [19].
Function-as-a-service (FaaS) is the predominant implementation of the serverless
model, decomposing applications into discrete, event-driven functions. These
functions activate in response to events such as HTTP requests, database updates,
or file uploads, enabling granular scalability and optimizing resource efficiency
significantly compared to traditional architectures [18–21].

**2.7.2** **Key Serverless Platforms**

Serverless computing gained significant momentum with Amazon Web Services’
introduction of AWS Lambda in 2014, establishing the foundational architecture
for mainstream FaaS implementations. Lambda offered developers automatic scaling and infrastructure-free execution triggered by specific events, rapidly becoming a blueprint for subsequent serverless platforms [17, 20].

Following AWS Lambda’s success, major cloud providers developed their
respective platforms. In 2016, Microsoft introduced Azure Functions, emphasizing
comprehensive integration across the Azure ecosystem and multilingual support. Simultaneously, Google launched Cloud Functions, targeting lightweight,
event-driven workloads seamlessly integrated within Google Cloud’s extensive
infrastructure [18, 21].

Additional noteworthy platforms include IBM Cloud Functions, developed
around the open-source Apache OpenWhisk project; Cloudflare Workers,
designed to execute functions at the network edge; and platform-neutral tools
like the Serverless Framework, simplifying cross-provider deployments. These
platforms collectively form a versatile ecosystem, enabling developers to select
environments best aligned with specific application requirements and technical
constraints [17–19].

_References_ **27**

**2.7.3** **Benefits and Limitations of Serverless Computing**

Serverless architectures provide significant advantages, driving widespread
adoption across various industry domains. The most immediate benefit is cost
efficiency, driven by a consumption-based pricing model eliminating payments
for idle capacity, notably advantageous for workloads with fluctuating demand.
Furthermore, automatic, rapid scalability from zero to high concurrency simplifies operational overhead, facilitating agile application development and quicker
deployment cycles [17, 19].

Nonetheless, serverless architectures possess inherent limitations. “ _Cold start_ ”
latency, representing delays in initializing function instances, remains problematic, particularly impacting latency-sensitive or infrequently executed functions.
Additionally, vendor lock-in emerges as a significant concern due to proprietary
APIs and deep integration within provider-specific ecosystems, complicating
migrations across cloud platforms. Moreover, the highly distributed nature of
serverless architectures amplifies complexity in monitoring, debugging, and maintaining observability, necessitating specialized tools and methodologies [24–26].

**2.8** **Conclusion**

The evolutionary transition from VMs to containerization and ultimately
to serverless computing underscores a clear progression toward heightened
abstraction and simplified operational management within cloud computing
paradigms. Each evolutionary step addressed specific limitations inherent in
prior approaches, reflecting iterative refinement and innovation.

Serverless computing, with its radical abstraction of infrastructure management, epitomizes the latest advancement in this sequence, substantially
influencing how applications are designed, implemented, and operated.
Future developments in serverless computing are anticipated to incorporate
automation-driven infrastructure management, further addressing existing
challenges like observability and vendor lock-in and enhancing interoperability
across diverse cloud ecosystems.

For researchers and industry practitioners alike, understanding these evolutionary dynamics is critical. It informs strategic technology adoption decisions,
ensuring that organizations can optimally leverage evolving cloud paradigms for
enhanced operational efficiency, scalability, and innovation.

**3.1** **Introduction**

Cloud-native computing and microservices architectures (MSAs) have become
a new focal point in current software engineering. These ideas appeared as a
result of a reaction to restrictions of old-fashioned monolithic applications, which
are prone to issues of scalability, maintainability, and deployment. With more
businesses moving toward cloud structures, there is also an increased demand
for software constructions that leverage the elasticity, resilience, and automation
features of the cloud. Microservices architectures, cloud-native, respond to
this challenge and break large applications into loosely coupled and separately
deployable services that can be developed, scaled, and maintained in an agile and
efficient way [1].

Cloud-native is not only closely related to the process of deploying applications
to cloud-based systems but also a series of principles and best practices that
take advantage of the distinctive opportunities of the cloud. These are containerization, orchestration, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD),
and infrastructure as code (IaC), and, collectively, they achieve fast delivery of
software and operation robustness. Microservices architecture goes hand-in-hand
with cloud-native, thus optimizing modularity, scalability, and fault isolation. This
architecture pattern breaks an application into a collection of mini-services, each
operating in its own process and cooperating through lightweight mechanisms,
usually HTTP Application Programming Interface (APIs).

Microservices are also important in the cloud-native space due to factors other
than scalability and agility. It promotes organizational alignment because services
can be owned and managed by small, cross-functional teams, and this enhances
the innovation occurrence with lower overhead costs of coordination. Also,

principles, and best practices regarding operations, the chapter will provide the

**3.2** **Fundamentals of Cloud-Native Computing**

Cloud-native computing is a paradigm shift toward software development and
deployment that alters the manner in which applications are created, deployed,
and managed. In contrast to the traditional way, when the software is created
to be used on a particular type of hardware or virtual machine, the cloud-native
applications are intended to make extensive use of the built-in benefits of the
cloud environment. Such strengths are on-demand resource provisioning, elastic
scalability, fault tolerance, and automation. The core values of cloud-native
computing are the basis of the new type of application architecture, such as
microservices [4].

Scalability is one of the most important convictions of cloud-native computing,
and it means that a system can help grow its workload by adjusting resources on
the fly. Cloud platforms offer elastic infrastructures such that applications can be
expanded horizontally (by adding more instances) and vertically (by increasing
resources, e.g., capacity). This elasticity guarantees that applications will be able to
retain performance and availability in the face of usage spikes except to the degree
of overprovisioning, thus reducing the cost of operations.

The other important principle is resilience, or always being there despite
failures. Cloud-native applications are made to expect and gracefully cancel
partial failures on the system. This is done by making use of redundancy, failover,
and self-healing properties inherent to cloud architecture and application design
practices. Fault tolerance is usually achieved with automated health checks, retry
policy, and circuit breakers.

Cloud-native applications also focus on automation in the software development
life cycle. Automation involves infrastructure provisioning, configuration management, deployment, testing, monitoring, and scaling. The tools able to deploy
versions of infrastructure in a repeatable fashion and enable version control on

**34** _3_ _Exploring Cloud-Native Microservices Architectures and Design Patterns_

the infrastructure called IaC are Terraform and Ansible. CI/CD pipelines speed up
and improve software delivery with the code integrations, testing, and deployment
done automatically, rather than manually [5].

The main technology that has facilitated cloud-native computing is containerization. Application code and dependencies are encapsulated in lightweight,
portable units called containers that can run in even the most diverse computing environments. Containers are created using tools that have become
standardized, such as Docker, and the deployment, scaling, and operations of a
containerized application are orchestrated by platforms like Kubernetes. In the
case of Kubernetes, specifically, the following features are not only important
but also compliant with cloud-native concepts: service discovery, load balancing,
automatic rollouts, and self-healing.

The decentralized governance and modularity are also encouraged through the
cloud-native model. Applications are designed into loosely connected components
or microservices that may be separately developed, deployed, and scaled. This kind
of modularity departs from the complexity linked with monolithic applications
and also promotes agile development. It is a heterogeneous tech stack; it allows
teams to pick the most effective tools and languages to use on particular services
without having an effect on the wider system [6]. Figure 3.2 illustrates the overview
of cloud-native principles.

Besides the technical ideals, cloud-native computing promotes organizational
and cultural changes. DevOps and site reliability engineering (SRE) are concepts
that have been adopted to mediate development and operations teams and encourage the distribution of application lifecycle and operational excellence. Monitoring
and logging, as well as observability during the design of applications, enables
identifying the problem before it occurs and effectively troubleshooting.

**Figure 3.2** Cloud-native
principles overview.

_3.2_ _Fundamentals of Cloud-Native Computing_ **35**

In cloud-native systems, security is cross-cutting. Cloud-native security
practices include identity and access management (IAM), secrets management,
network segmentation, and runtime security policies. It is necessary to secure
container images, orchestrator configurations, and continuous delivery pipelines
to limit the risks in dynamic and distributed settings. Figure 3.3 provides container
and Kubernetes ecosystem.

To sum up, cloud-native computing is defined by its orientation to draw on
capabilities of the cloud infrastructure to develop the applications that are scalable, resilient, automated, and modular. The combined essence of these principles
enables an organization to adjust quickly to the varying needs of the business
in the context of high reliability and efficiency. These underlying principles are
necessary to comprehend in order to build and host MSAs, achieving the potential
of cloud-native paradigms [7].

**Figure 3.3** Container and Kubernetes ecosystem.

**36** _3_ _Exploring Cloud-Native Microservices Architectures and Design Patterns_

**3.3** **Microservices Architecture (MSA) Overview**

MSA is a style of application architecture that organizes applications into small
services, which are autonomous and individually capable of business functions.
This is in direct contrast to the traditional monolithic architecture, where
construction of the application would be made as a single indivisible unit. The
requirement of enhanced agility, scalability, and resilience of software systems
has spurred the development of the MSA in large part as applied to the world of
cloud-based systems.

In its most basic form, MSA is passionate about embracing the concept of
decomposition by breaking down complex applications into manageable components that are able to be developed, deployed, and maintained additionally. Every
microservice can contain a specific custom functionality and has its data and
state, which improves high modularity and loose coupling. This isolation enables
the independent development by different teams and reduces time to market and
ease of maintenance.

Among the main benefits of microservices, one can list independent deployability. With microservices, as compared to monolithic systems, in which a
minor alteration necessitates redeployment of the whole app, an individual
microservice can be swapped, upgraded, or scaled without affecting the rest of
the microservices. The lower granularity lowers risk and supports continuous
delivery and incremental upgrades, which are key in rapid development.

Scalability is also increased since with MSA a service is able to scale independently with regard to its own resource requirement. It is possible to scale out
services with increased loads without fueling the capacity of lesser important
components unnecessarily. This precision scalability enhances better usage of
the resource and lowers the operation costs, particularly when run on the elastic
cloud structure. Figure 3.4 represents the comparison between microservices and
monolithic architecture.

Although there are positive aspects about MSA, the technology is associated
with a number of challenges. Microservices have a distributed architecture, which
results in added complexity on the operation front. Through networks, services
are communicating along with the associated latency, points of possible failure,
and a need to have strong interservice communication protocols. Moreover, data
consistency between services is complicated because they have decentralized ownership, and the patterns like eventual consistency and sagas are used to distribute
transactions.

In MSA, security matters are also more complex. The large attack surface
caused by the large number of services demands secure authentication, authorization, and encryption capabilities at the service-to-service scope. Moreover,

realize observability in distributed elements and to diagnose problems in them [8].

In order to better deal with these complexities, one of the solutions deployed
by organizations is the service discovery mechanism and API gateways. Service
discovery allows dynamic service location and load balancing, and an API

services to the clients; hence, it allows cross-cutting concerns like authentication,
rate limiters, and request routing. The communication patterns of microservices
